# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES physiological logging.** ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al. 1992) is the canonical WAL framework. Log records are *physiological*: physical to a page (identified by pageID), logical within it (e.g., "insert tuple into slot array"), which tolerates intra-page reorganization during redo. Every page carries a **pageLSN** (the LSN of the last log record that modified it), and the **WAL protocol** requires that a dirty page may not be written to stable storage until all log records up to its pageLSN are forced (flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN). Commit requires forcing the log up to the transaction's commit record (**force-log-at-commit**), while data pages themselves follow a **no-force / steal** buffer policy — dirty pages may be evicted before commit (steal) and need not be flushed at commit (no-force) — which is precisely what necessitates both redo and undo logging. Each log record carries a **prevLSN** back-pointer, chaining a transaction's records for rollback.

**Group commit.** Because every commit requires an fsync of the log, naïve per-transaction flushing serializes throughput on storage latency. Group commit batches the commit records of many concurrently committing transactions into a single log force, amortizing the fsync. InnoDB implements this around its redo log mutex; PostgreSQL exposes `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings` to tune the batching window. A related relaxation is **asynchronous commit** (PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit = off`), which acknowledges commit before the flush, trading a bounded window of durability loss for latency.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes vs. the doublewrite buffer.** Physiological redo assumes the page it replays against is internally consistent; a crash mid-way through a partial (torn) sector-level page write violates that. PostgreSQL uses **full-page writes (FPW)**: the first modification to a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page image, so redo can restore it wholesale. InnoDB instead uses the **doublewrite buffer**: dirty pages are first written sequentially to a dedicated doublewrite area, fsynced, then written in place; on recovery a torn page is repaired from the doublewrite copy. FPW inflates WAL volume after checkpoints; doublewrite roughly doubles data-write bandwidth but keeps the redo log compact.

**Fuzzy checkpointing.** To bound recovery time without quiescing the system, ARIES-style systems take *fuzzy* checkpoints: a checkpoint record captures the **Active Transaction Table (ATT)** and **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — the latter recording each dirty page's **recLSN** (the earliest LSN that may need redo) — without flushing pages synchronously. Recovery's redo scan can then begin at min(recLSN) rather than the log's origin. The master record points at the most recent complete checkpoint.

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**PostgreSQL tuple-level versioning (xmin/xmax + VACUUM).** PostgreSQL stores versions in-place in the heap: each tuple header carries **xmin** (creating XID) and **xmax** (deleting/updating XID). An UPDATE is a delete+insert, chaining versions via `t_ctid` (optimized by **HOT — heap-only tuples** — when no indexed column changes, avoiding index churn). A transaction's **snapshot** (xmin horizon, xmax, in-progress XID list) plus commit status from the CLOG (pg_xact) determines visibility. Dead versions are reclaimed by **VACUUM**, which also freezes old XIDs to prevent 32-bit **transaction ID wraparound**. The cost profile: reads never block writes, but garbage accumulates in the heap ("bloat").

**InnoDB/Oracle undo-based consistent reads (rollback segments).** InnoDB and Oracle keep only the newest version in place; readers reconstruct older versions by walking **undo log** records in **rollback segments** backwards from the current row (each row carries a roll pointer and the trx ID). An InnoDB **read view** captures the set of active transaction IDs at snapshot time; a reader applies undo until it reaches a version visible to its view. The **purge** thread garbage-collects undo once no read view can need it ("history list length" measures the backlog). Oracle's equivalent failure mode is the classic **ORA-01555 "snapshot too old"** when undo is recycled before a long-running query finishes.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation admits **write skew** (two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint data, jointly violating an invariant). SSI (Cahill et al. 2008; Ports & Grittner's PostgreSQL implementation, 9.1+) tracks **rw-antidependencies** via SIREAD locks (predicate-ish read markers): a serialization anomaly requires a "dangerous structure" of two consecutive rw-antidependency edges (T1 →rw T2 →rw T3 with T3 committing first), and SSI aborts one participant when such a structure forms. This yields true serializability with optimistic, mostly non-blocking behavior, at the cost of false-positive aborts.

**Timestamp-ordered in-memory MVCC (Hekaton).** Microsoft Hekaton (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP) is a lock-free, latch-free MVCC design: versions carry begin/end timestamps, installed via atomic compare-and-swap; transactions get begin and commit timestamps from a monotonic counter and run a **validation phase** (re-check read set visibility at commit time) for serializable mode, with **commit dependencies** allowing speculative reads of uncommitted versions. Garbage collection is cooperative — threads unlink versions whose end timestamps precede the oldest active transaction.

## 3. Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees

**Memtable → SSTable pipeline.** Writes land in an in-memory, sorted **memtable** (typically a skip list in RocksDB/LevelDB) after being appended to a WAL for durability. When full, the memtable is sealed (becomes **immutable memtable**) and flushed as a sorted, immutable **SSTable** with a block index and footer. Reads must merge the memtable, immutable memtables, and SSTables newest-to-oldest; deletes are logical **tombstones** that must survive compaction until they can be proven to mask nothing in lower levels.

**Compaction policies: leveled vs. size-tiered.** **Leveled compaction (LCS)**, as in LevelDB/RocksDB, organizes levels L1…Ln with exponentially growing capacity (fanout ~10) where each level is a single sorted run with non-overlapping key ranges; compaction merges an L_i file into overlapping L_{i+1} files. This minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and bounds read amplification (one file per level) but has high **write amplification** (≈ fanout × levels). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS, Cassandra)** merges SSTables of similar size into bigger ones: low write amplification, but high space amplification (up to 2× transiently) and many overlapping runs to check on reads. The **RUM conjecture** formalizes this three-way tension among read, update (write), and memory/space amplification; RocksDB's **universal compaction** and Cassandra's TWCS (time-windowed, for TTL data) are intermediate points.

**Bloom filters and fence pointers.** Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** over its keys so point lookups can skip tables with high probability (~1% false positive at ~10 bits/key); RocksDB supports prefix Bloom filters for bounded-prefix range scans. **Fence pointers** (per-block index entries) restrict a within-file search to one block. Monkey (Dasu et al./Dayan et al., 2017) showed that optimally allocating Bloom-filter bits non-uniformly across levels (more bits to smaller levels) improves the lookup cost curve.

**Key–value separation (WiscKey).** WiscKey (Lu et al., FAST 2016) stores values in a separate append-only **vLog** and keeps only keys+pointers in the LSM, slashing write amplification for large values since compaction no longer rewrites values — at the cost of an extra indirection on reads, vLog garbage collection, and degraded range-scan locality (mitigated on SSDs by parallel random reads). RocksDB's **BlobDB** and Titan are production descendants.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Splits, merges, and redistribution.** Insertion into a full leaf triggers a **node split**: half the entries move to a new right sibling and a **separator key** is promoted to the parent, possibly cascading up to a root split (the only way a B+tree grows in height, preserving perfect balance). Deletions that drop a node below the minimum fill (~50%) trigger either **redistribution (borrowing)** from an adjacent sibling with an updated separator, or a **merge (coalescing)** with the sibling and removal of the parent's separator. Many production engines (e.g., PostgreSQL nbtree historically) lazily defer merges, only reclaiming fully empty pages, since merge-heavy workloads are rare and merges complicate concurrency. **Fill factor** tuning (e.g., 90% default leaf fill in PostgreSQL) leaves split headroom; right-most splits are special-cased (split 100/0 rather than 50/50) to optimize monotonically increasing keys.

**Latch coupling and Blink-trees.** Concurrent access classically uses **latch coupling (crabbing)**: acquire the child's latch before releasing the parent's, releasing ancestors once a node is "safe" (won't split/merge). Pessimistic descent write-latches the whole path; **optimistic lock coupling** (Leis et al.) uses version counters and restarts instead. The **Blink-tree** (Lehman & Yao 1981) adds a **right-link pointer** and **high key** to every node so that a reader racing a concurrent split can detect "my key exceeds this node's high key" and chase the right-link — eliminating the need to hold multiple latches during descent. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Blink-tree variant.

**Structure-modification operations (SMOs) and logging/recovery interaction.** Splits/merges are multi-page atomic operations that must be crash-safe. ARIES/IM and ARIES/KVL treat SMOs with **nested top actions**: the SMO's effects are made permanent (via a dummy CLR) even if the enclosing transaction later aborts, so logical undo of the key insert can proceed against the new tree shape. InnoDB similarly uses mini-transactions (mtr) to make each SMO an atomic redo unit.

**Write-optimized variants: Bw-trees and fractal trees.** The **Bw-tree** (Levandoski et al., Microsoft Hekaton/DocumentDB) is latch-free: logical page IDs resolve through a **mapping table**, and updates are prepended as **delta records** installed by CAS, periodically consolidated; splits are broken into two CAS steps using Blink-style side links. **Fractal trees / Bε-trees** (TokuDB/PerconaFT) place per-node **message buffers** that batch inserts and flush downward lazily, converting random insert I/O into large amortized writes — an in-place analogue of LSM write optimization. **Prefix and suffix truncation** (Bayer & Unterauer) compress separator keys to raise fanout; **bulk loading** builds the tree bottom-up from sorted input at a chosen fill factor instead of repeated top-down inserts.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**The basic protocol and its blocking problem.** 2PC splits atomic commitment into a **prepare (voting) phase** — the coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant force-writes a prepare record and votes YES (entering the **prepared/in-doubt state**, relinquishing its unilateral right to abort) or NO — and a **commit phase**, where the coordinator force-writes its commit/abort decision and disseminates it; participants ack after logging the outcome. The protocol's fundamental weakness is **blocking**: if the coordinator fails after participants prepare, they must hold locks and wait (the **in-doubt window**); cooperative termination (asking peers) helps only if some peer saw the decision. This is the practical face of the two-generals/FLP-style impossibility of non-blocking commit with unreliable links and crashes.

**Presumed abort and presumed commit.** These are logging/messaging optimizations from R* (Mohan, Lindsay, Obermarck). **Presumed abort** (the de facto standard, codified in the X/Open **XA** interface): the coordinator may forget a transaction after deciding abort without forcing an abort record; a participant inquiring about an unknown transaction is told "abort." This eliminates abort-path forces and ACKs, and allows the **read-only optimization** (a read-only participant votes READ-ONLY and drops out after phase one). **Presumed commit** inverts the presumption, saving a round on the commit path but requiring the coordinator to force a record *before* the prepare phase, so it is rarely the default.

**Non-blocking and consensus-based commit: 3PC and Paxos Commit.** **Three-phase commit (Skeen)** inserts a pre-commit state so no participant commits while another could still abort, making the protocol non-blocking under crash-stop failures with a synchronous network — but it is unsafe under network partitions, so it saw little production use. **Paxos Commit (Gray & Lamport 2006)** replaces the single coordinator with a Paxos consensus instance per participant vote: the commit decision is a function of 2F+1 acceptors' state, tolerating F failures without blocking, and degenerating to 2PC when F=0. **Spanner** operationalizes this layering: each participant is itself a Paxos-replicated group, the 2PC coordinator state is replicated in its own Paxos group, and coordinator failover is thus transparent — 2PC *over* consensus rather than instead of it. Calvin/deterministic databases and single-shard designs represent the alternative strategy of avoiding 2PC altogether.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport clocks and happened-before.** Lamport's 1978 paper defines the **happened-before** partial order (→): program order, plus send-before-receive, closed transitively; concurrent events are those unordered by →. A **Lamport clock** is a scalar counter: increment on each local event; on message receipt set C := max(C, C_msg) + 1. It guarantees e → f ⟹ C(e) < C(f) (consistency with causality) but not the converse — C(e) < C(f) does not imply causal order — so Lamport clocks can create a total order (tie-break by node ID) but cannot *detect* concurrency. They underpin timestamp-ordering concurrency control and deterministic tie-breaking throughout distributed databases.

**Vector clocks and version vectors.** A **vector clock** carries one counter per node; merging takes the element-wise max. They are *strongly consistent with causality*: VC(e) < VC(f) ⟺ e → f, and incomparable vectors identify genuinely **concurrent** updates. **Amazon Dynamo** used per-object **version vectors** to detect conflicting replicas and surface **sibling** versions to the application for semantic reconciliation (Riak retained this; stock DynamoDB moved to last-writer-wins). Costs: O(n) metadata, actor-ID management, and pruning hazards (Dynamo truncated vectors, risking false concurrency). **Dotted version vectors** fix the sibling-explosion artifacts of server-side versioning.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni, Demirbas et al. 2014) combines a physical component (max observed wall clock) and a logical component (counter breaking ties within the same physical value), in fixed 64-bit-ish space. HLC is consistent with happened-before like a Lamport clock, yet stays within a bounded offset of physical time, so timestamps are human-meaningful and usable for snapshots. **CockroachDB** uses HLC for MVCC timestamps: a reader encountering a value within its **max-offset uncertainty window** must perform an **uncertainty restart** at a higher timestamp — logical causality patching over imperfect clock synchronization.

**TrueTime: bounded-uncertainty physical clocks.** Spanner's **TrueTime** API returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain true time, backed by GPS and atomic clocks (ε typically < 7ms). **Commit wait** — the coordinator waits until TT.after(commit_ts) before releasing locks/acknowledging — ensures that timestamp order equals real-time order, yielding **external consistency (strict serializability)** and lock-free consistent snapshot reads across the globe. Conceptually, TrueTime shows that shrinking clock uncertainty converts a logical-ordering problem into a (short) waiting problem; HLC is the engineering answer when you lack dedicated time infrastructure.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Majority read/write quorums (R + W > N).** In the classic replicated-data quorum scheme (Gifford's weighted voting, 1979), a write must be acknowledged by W of N replicas and a read must contact R, with **R + W > N** guaranteeing read/write quorum intersection (any read sees at least one latest-write replica, selected by version/timestamp) and **W > N/2** preventing conflicting concurrent writes. **Dynamo-style stores** (Cassandra, Riak) expose tunable per-operation consistency (ONE/QUORUM/ALL); note that R+W>N alone gives read-your-latest-acknowledged-write intersection, *not* linearizability, absent careful read-repair/write-back semantics. Complementary anti-entropy machinery — **read repair** and **Merkle-tree synchronization** — converges replicas that quorums skipped.

**Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff.** Dynamo's availability-first variant: if home replicas are unreachable, writes go to the next healthy nodes on the consistent-hashing ring, each holding a **hint** that is handed off to the proper owner upon recovery. This keeps writes available during partitions but **breaks the intersection guarantee** — a sloppy read quorum may miss a sloppy write quorum — so it trades consistency for durability/availability and relies on version vectors plus anti-entropy to reconverge.

**Consensus quorums (Paxos/Raft) and Flexible Paxos.** Majority quorums in **Paxos/Raft** serve a different purpose than replica-register quorums: any two majorities intersect, so a new leader's quorum necessarily includes a node that saw any previously **chosen/committed** entry — this intersection is the safety core of leader election and log commitment (Raft additionally commits only entries from the leader's current term directly, per its commitment rule). **Flexible Paxos (FPaxos, Howard et al. 2016)** proves the requirement is only that *phase-1 (leader-election) quorums intersect phase-2 (replication) quorums* — Q1 + Q2 > N — not that replication quorums intersect each other; e.g., with N=5, replicate to 2 and elect with 4, improving steady-state latency/throughput at the cost of harder failover. **Grid quorums** instantiate the same idea geometrically (rows for one phase, columns for the other).

**Witnesses and hierarchical/weighted schemes.** **Witness replicas** (Paris 1986; used in Spanner, etcd "learners" differ, Oracle/vSAN witness nodes) vote in quorums without storing full data, cheaply breaking ties across failure domains (classic 2+2+witness across three sites). **Hierarchical quorums** (Kumar) and weighted voting reduce quorum sizes to O(√N) or bias toward well-provisioned nodes; leases/leader reads (as in Raft **lease-based reads** or Spanner leader leases) let systems serve linearizable reads from one node by converting a time bound into an implicit quorum.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** On restart, ARIES runs: (i) **Analysis** — scan forward from the last checkpoint to rebuild the ATT (loser transactions) and DPT, establishing the redo start point (min recLSN); (ii) **Redo** — "**repeating history**": reapply *all* updates (including those of losers) where pageLSN < record LSN, restoring the exact pre-crash state — this is the key ARIES insight, decoupling redo from transaction outcomes; (iii) **Undo** — roll back losers by following prevLSN chains in reverse LSN order, writing a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)** for each undone action. CLRs are **redo-only** and carry an **UndoNxtLSN** pointer skipping already-undone work, which makes recovery **idempotent** under repeated crashes (crash-during-recovery never re-undoes or re-does compensation). Fuzzy checkpoints (ATT+DPT snapshots) bound the analysis/redo scan without quiescing.

**Shadow paging.** System R's recovery alternative: updates go to **shadow (copied) pages**; a page table maps logical to physical pages, and commit atomically swaps the root pointer to the new page table — the old version remains intact until the swap, so recovery is trivial (discard uncommitted shadows). Costs that killed it for high-performance OLTP: data fragmentation (destroyed clustering), page-table overhead, and no support for page-level concurrent transactions — but the idea survives in **copy-on-write B-trees** (LMDB, btrfs, ZFS) and SQLite's rollback-journal/WAL duality. LMDB notably needs *no* recovery phase at all: a crash simply leaves the last committed root reachable.

**InnoDB redo+undo recovery.** InnoDB recovery is a concrete ARIES descendant with a twist: the **redo log** (circular ib_logfile / redo segments, physiological **mini-transaction (mtr)** records) is replayed from the last checkpoint LSN to the log head, with torn pages first repaired from the **doublewrite buffer**; then uncommitted transactions are rolled back using **undo logs** stored *as data* in rollback segments (undo is itself redo-logged, so it's recoverable). Rollback of losers proceeds in the background after the database opens, shortening perceived downtime. Binlog–redo consistency for replication is itself sealed with an internal 2PC between the storage engine and the binary log (XA between InnoDB and binlog).

**Log replay in no-undo architectures and distributed recovery.** PostgreSQL illustrates a **redo-only** recovery design: because MVCC retains old tuple versions in the heap (no in-place overwrite requiring undo), crash recovery is a pure WAL redo from the last checkpoint's redo pointer, with full-page images fixing torn pages; "rollback" is merely marking the XID aborted in pg_xact. The same replay machinery drives **point-in-time recovery (PITR)** from base backups + archived WAL and streaming **physical replication** — recovery, backup restore, and replication unify as "log shipping + replay." In replicated-state-machine systems (Raft/Paxos), recovery generalizes further: a restarted node replays its durable log and catches up from the leader, with **snapshots/log compaction** bounding replay length — the distributed analogue of checkpointing.

---

**Synthesis.** A unifying lens: all eight areas are instances of ordering + durability + redundancy. WAL and ARIES impose a durable total order (LSNs) on updates so that recovery can deterministically repeat history; MVCC and logical clocks generalize ordering to *versions* and *causality* so readers never block writers; LSM trees and B+trees are the two poles of the write-vs-read amplification tradeoff for maintaining sorted durable state; and 2PC plus quorum intersection extend single-node atomicity and durability across machines — with modern systems (Spanner, CockroachDB) explicitly layering 2PC over consensus quorums and stitching timestamps to real time (TrueTime/HLC) to recover serializable semantics at global scale.

# Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and Crash Recovery: Technical Findings

## Part 1: Write-Ahead Logging

### 1.1 The WAL Protocol (Core Invariants)

Write-ahead logging enforces two rules:

1. **WAL rule (undo rule / flush-before-page-write):** Before a dirty page containing uncommitted changes may be written to the database on stable storage, all log records describing those changes (including undo information) must be forced to the log. Formally: a page P with pageLSN = L may not be written back until the log is durable up through L (`flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN(P)`).
2. **Commit rule (force-log-at-commit / redo rule):** A transaction is not considered committed until all of its log records, up to and including its commit record, are on stable storage.

Together these implement **steal / no-force** buffer management: the buffer manager may *steal* frames (evict dirty pages of uncommitted transactions — requires undo logging) and need not *force* dirty pages at commit (requires redo logging). Steal/no-force is the highest-performance policy quadrant and is what ARIES was designed for.

### 1.2 ARIES-Style Physiological Logging

ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics; Mohan et al., IBM, 1992) uses **physiological logging**: log records are *physical to a page, logical within a page*. A record identifies the page (physical) but describes the change as an operation on that page (e.g., "insert tuple into slot k"), not raw byte diffs of the whole page. This contrasts with:

- **Physical (value) logging:** before-image/after-image byte ranges — simple, idempotent, but large and incompatible with logical operations like page compaction.
- **Logical (operation) logging:** "insert key K into index I" — compact, but redo/undo cannot be applied unless the database is action-consistent; hard to make redo idempotent.

Physiological logging gets compactness while keeping page-granular redo correctness, because redo is made conditional on the **pageLSN** (see below), making replay effectively idempotent.

Key log record structure: `⟨LSN, transID, prevLSN, pageID, redo-info, undo-info⟩`. The **prevLSN** field chains each transaction's records into a backward-linked list, enabling efficient undo of a single transaction.

### 1.3 LSN Ordering

The **Log Sequence Number (LSN)** is a monotonically increasing identifier, typically the byte offset of the record in the log. LSNs appear in several places:

- **pageLSN:** stored in each page header; the LSN of the most recent log record that modified the page. During redo, a logged update is reapplied **only if pageLSN < LSN of the log record** — this is the exactly-once semantics that makes physiological redo safe.
- **flushedLSN:** in-memory; the largest LSN durably written to the log. The WAL rule is enforced as `pageLSN ≤ flushedLSN` before page writeback.
- **recLSN (recovery LSN):** in the Dirty Page Table; the LSN of the first record that dirtied the page since it was last flushed — the earliest point from which redo for that page might be needed.
- **lastLSN:** in the Transaction Table; the most recent record written by each transaction.
- **undoNextLSN:** in Compensation Log Records; points to the next record to undo (see §2.1).

### 1.4 Group Commit

Forcing the log at every commit costs one synchronous device write (fsync) per transaction. **Group commit** amortizes this: the system briefly delays commit acknowledgment, batching the commit records of multiple concurrent transactions into a single log flush. One fsync durably commits many transactions, raising throughput by orders of magnitude at a small latency cost. Implementations: PostgreSQL (`commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`, plus implicit batching in the WAL writer), MySQL/InnoDB binary-log group commit (three-stage flush/sync/commit pipeline that also preserves binlog–redo ordering for replication), and most modern engines. Group commit interacts with LSN ordering trivially: a single flush to LSN *L* commits every transaction whose commit record has LSN ≤ *L*.

### 1.5 Torn-Page Protection: PostgreSQL Full-Page Writes vs. InnoDB Doublewrite Buffer

Database pages (8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB default in InnoDB) exceed the storage device's atomic write unit (traditionally a 512 B or 4 KB sector). A crash mid-write yields a **torn page** (partial write / fractured block) — part old, part new — which physiological redo cannot repair because the page is internally inconsistent and its pageLSN may be garbage.

- **PostgreSQL full-page writes (FPW, a.k.a. full-page images):** The *first* time a page is modified after each checkpoint, PostgreSQL logs the entire page image into the WAL instead of just the tuple-level delta. During recovery, redo restores the full image unconditionally, overwriting any torn state; subsequent delta records then apply on top. Cost: WAL volume spikes after checkpoints (motivating longer checkpoint intervals and WAL compression, `wal_compression`). FPW can be disabled only on filesystems/devices guaranteeing atomic page writes (e.g., ZFS).

- **InnoDB doublewrite buffer:** InnoDB keeps the redo log small (physiological) and instead protects pages at flush time. Before writing dirty pages to their final tablespace locations, InnoDB first writes them sequentially to a **doublewrite buffer** (a dedicated on-disk area; separate doublewrite files since MySQL 8.0.20), fsyncs it, then writes the pages in place. On recovery, any torn page in the tablespace (detected by checksum) is restored from its intact copy in the doublewrite area, after which redo proceeds normally. Cost: each page is physically written twice, but the doublewrite write is sequential and batched, so overhead is typically modest (~5–10%). Disabled when atomic writes are available (e.g., on certain NVMe/filesystem combinations).

Trade-off summary: FPW pushes the cost into the log stream (log volume, replication traffic); doublewrite pushes it into the data-write path (I/O bandwidth).

### 1.6 Checkpointing

Checkpoints bound recovery time by limiting how far back redo must scan.

- **Sharp (consistent) checkpoint:** quiesce updates, flush all dirty pages, then log the checkpoint. Simple but stalls the system; rarely used in modern engines.
- **Fuzzy checkpoint (ARIES):** no quiescence. The system writes a `begin_checkpoint` record, then an `end_checkpoint` record containing snapshots of the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — (pageID, recLSN) pairs for pages dirty in the buffer pool — and the **Active Transaction Table (ATT/XT)** — (transID, status, lastLSN) for in-flight transactions. The **master record** at a fixed log/disk location points to the latest complete checkpoint. No pages need be flushed at checkpoint time; the DPT's minimum recLSN tells recovery where redo must begin. In practice, background writers continuously flush dirty pages so the min-recLSN advances.
- **InnoDB checkpointing:** fuzzy, driven by the circular redo log — the **checkpoint LSN** advances as dirty pages are flushed in (approximately) flush-list/oldest-modification order; redo log records older than the checkpoint LSN can be overwritten. Flushing is paced ("adaptive flushing") to avoid log-full stalls.
- **PostgreSQL checkpoints:** periodic flush of all dirty shared buffers plus a checkpoint WAL record; spread over time (`checkpoint_completion_target`) to avoid I/O spikes. After a checkpoint completes, older WAL segments are recyclable and FPW "first touch" flags reset.

---

## Part 2: Crash Recovery

### 2.1 ARIES Three-Phase Recovery

ARIES's central principle is **repeating history**: on restart, bring the database to the exact state it had at the moment of the crash (including uncommitted changes), *then* undo losers. Three phases over the log:

**Phase 1 — Analysis.** Start from the last complete checkpoint (via the master record). Scan forward to the end of the log, reconstructing:
- the **ATT**: transactions active at crash (adding transactions that started after the checkpoint, removing those that ended) — these are the **loser transactions** to undo;
- the **DPT**: pages possibly dirty at crash, each with its recLSN (adding pages first dirtied after the checkpoint).

Outputs: the redo start point (**min recLSN over the DPT**) and the undo set (losers with their lastLSNs).

**Phase 2 — Redo (repeating history).** Scan forward from min(recLSN). For each updating log record (including CLRs — CLRs are redone too), reapply the change **iff**: the page is in the DPT, the record's LSN ≥ the page's recLSN, and the on-disk **pageLSN < record LSN**. The pageLSN test guarantees idempotent, exactly-once application. At the end of redo, the database state equals the pre-crash state. Both committed and uncommitted work is present — this is what "repeating history" means, and it's what makes fine-grained (record-level) locking and logical undo safe.

**Phase 3 — Undo with CLRs.** Roll back all losers by following their prevLSN chains backward (processed together, in descending LSN order across all losers). For each undone update, write a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**: a redo-only record describing the undo action, carrying an **undoNextLSN** pointer = the prevLSN of the record just undone. Properties:
- CLRs are **never undone** (redo-only), so undo work is never undone — bounding the log growth during repeated crash/restart cycles (undo makes forward progress across crashes).
- If a crash occurs mid-undo, recovery resumes undo at the undoNextLSN of the last CLR, skipping already-compensated records — restart is idempotent.
- When a loser's undoNextLSN chain reaches null, an `end` (abort-complete) record is written.

ARIES also supports **nested top actions** (e.g., B-tree structure modifications that must persist even if the enclosing transaction aborts) via a dummy CLR whose undoNextLSN skips the action's records, and **savepoints/partial rollback** using the same CLR machinery.

### 2.2 Shadow Paging (System R)

The historical alternative, used in System R's recovery manager (Lorie, 1977): maintain two page tables — the **current page table** (volatile, reflecting in-flight updates) and the **shadow page table** (on disk, reflecting the last consistent state). Updates use **copy-on-write**: a modified page is written to a *new* disk location; the current page table is updated to point to it, while the shadow table still points to the old version. Commit = atomically installing the current page table as the new shadow (one atomic write of the root/master pointer). Crash recovery is trivial: discard current state, resume from the shadow table — **no redo and no undo scan is required** (NO-STEAL/FORCE-like semantics at the page-table level).

Drawbacks (why ARIES-style WAL won):
- **Data fragmentation / loss of clustering** — pages migrate on every write, destroying sequential layout.
- **Garbage collection** of superseded pages.
- **Commit cost** — flushing the page table and changed pages; poor concurrency (System R combined shadowing with logging precisely because shadowing alone couldn't support record-level locking and high concurrency well).
- Hard to scale to multi-transaction concurrent commit.

Shadow paging survives in modern forms: **copy-on-write B-trees** (LMDB, btrfs, ZFS's transactional object model), and SQLite's optional rollback-journal vs. WAL modes echo the same design space.

### 2.3 InnoDB Recovery: Redo Log + Undo Logs

InnoDB splits ARIES's single log into two structures:

- **Redo log:** a circular, fixed-size physiological log (mini-transaction, "mtr", records such as `MLOG_REC_INSERT`), identified by LSN. Enforces the WAL rule; group-committed; bounded by the checkpoint LSN.
- **Undo logs:** before-images stored as **rollback segments inside the database itself** (undo tablespaces), as regular pages — therefore undo data is itself protected by the redo log. Undo records double as the **version store for MVCC** (consistent reads reconstruct old row versions by walking undo chains via each row's roll pointer).

Recovery sequence on restart:
1. **Torn-page repair:** restore any corrupted pages from the doublewrite buffer (checksum-verified).
2. **Redo phase:** scan the redo log from the last checkpoint LSN; parse records into a hash table keyed by page; apply to pages (pageLSN-guarded), repeating history. This includes redoing changes to undo-log pages.
3. **Undo phase:** reconstruct the transaction system state from rollback segments; transactions that were active (not committed/prepared-resolved) at crash are rolled back using their undo records. Notably, after redo completes InnoDB can **open for new transactions while loser rollback proceeds in the background** — because undo records are in the database proper, background rollback is an ordinary transactional activity. XA/binlog two-phase transactions in PREPARED state are resolved against the binary log (commit if the binlog contains them, else roll back).
4. Undo records are later **purged** once no read view can need them.

Structurally this is ARIES with: physiological redo, repeating history, and undo-as-data (rather than undo records interleaved in the log with CLRs; InnoDB's rollback is itself redo-logged, achieving the same "undo survives crashes" property as CLRs).

### 2.4 Log-Structured Recovery

In **log-structured systems**, the log *is* the database, so recovery changes shape:

- **LSM-tree engines (LevelDB/RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase):** writes go to a WAL (commit log) + in-memory memtable; memtables are flushed as immutable SSTables. Recovery = replay the WAL segments newer than the last flushed memtable to rebuild the memtable; SSTables are immutable and never need redo/undo. A **MANIFEST/version log** (itself a log) records SSTable set changes atomically; recovery replays it to reconstruct the LSM version. No undo phase exists at the storage layer — visibility/atomicity is handled by sequence numbers (snapshots) and atomic WriteBatches, so partially written batches are simply not replayed (detected via per-record checksums; torn tail truncated).
- **Log-structured file systems (Rosenblum & Ousterhout's LFS):** recovery = roll forward from the last checkpoint through the segment log, using segment summary blocks; cost of cleaning (GC) replaces cost of undo.
- **PostgreSQL archive/streaming recovery and point-in-time recovery (PITR)** generalize redo-only recovery: a base backup plus continuous WAL replay to any LSN — the same redo machinery as crash recovery, with no undo phase because PostgreSQL's MVCC leaves aborted tuples in place (vacuum reclaims them) — i.e., PostgreSQL is effectively a **no-undo/redo** (NO-STEAL is not required; aborted data is invisible via xact status in the CLOG/pg_xact rather than physically undone).
- **NVM/distributed variants:** write-behind logging (WBL) for persistent memory, and replicated state machines (Raft log replay) apply the same pattern — a durable ordered log plus deterministic replay from a snapshot/checkpoint.

The unifying contrast: ARIES recovers *pages* via redo+undo; log-structured designs recover *state* via redo-only replay over immutable data, trading undo complexity for compaction/garbage-collection cost.

---

## Named Mechanisms Index

**WAL (≥3):** physiological logging; WAL/flush-before-page-write + force-log-at-commit rules; LSN/pageLSN/flushedLSN/recLSN ordering; group commit; full-page writes (PostgreSQL); doublewrite buffer (InnoDB); fuzzy checkpoints with DPT/ATT and master record.

**Crash recovery (≥3):** ARIES three-phase recovery (analysis, redo/repeating history, undo with CLRs and undoNextLSN, nested top actions); shadow paging (System R, shadow/current page tables, atomic root switch); InnoDB recovery (doublewrite repair → redo from checkpoint LSN → background rollback via undo tablespaces, binlog-coordinated XA resolution); log-structured recovery (LSM WAL+memtable replay, MANIFEST replay, LFS roll-forward, PITR redo-only replay).

# MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

MVCC lets readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers (and vice versa) by retaining multiple physical versions of each logical data item. Key design axes: where old versions live (in-place vs. append-only vs. undo chains), how visibility is decided (transaction IDs vs. timestamps), and how obsolete versions are reclaimed (vacuum vs. purge).

## 1. PostgreSQL: xmin/xmax tuple versioning + snapshots + VACUUM

**Version storage.** PostgreSQL is append-only at the tuple level: an UPDATE creates a whole new tuple version in the heap; the old version stays in place. Each heap tuple header carries:

- **xmin**: the XID (32-bit transaction ID) of the inserting transaction.
- **xmax**: the XID of the deleting/updating transaction (0/invalid if live). xmax is also used for row-level locks (via MultiXacts when multiple lockers exist).
- **ctid / t_ctid**: forms the forward-pointing update chain from old version to new version (HOT chains keep intra-page updates off the indexes when no indexed column changes).
- Hint bits (`HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, etc.) cache commit status to avoid repeated **pg_xact** (commit log, formerly clog) lookups.

**Visibility via snapshots.** A snapshot is `(xmin, xmax, xip[])`: all XIDs < snapshot-xmin are definitively finished; XIDs ≥ snapshot-xmax are invisible; `xip[]` lists in-progress XIDs in between. A tuple is visible iff its xmin is committed and visible to the snapshot, and its xmax is absent, aborted, or not yet visible. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE take one snapshot per transaction (snapshot isolation semantics; serializability layered on via SSI, below).

**VACUUM.** Dead versions (deleted/superseded tuples invisible to every snapshot) must be garbage-collected. VACUUM removes tuples older than the global **xmin horizon** (oldest snapshot across backends, replication slots, prepared transactions — any of which can cause bloat if held long). VACUUM also performs **freezing**: because XIDs are 32-bit and compared modulo-2³¹, old xmin values are marked frozen (via `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` / historically FrozenTransactionId) to prevent **transaction ID wraparound**. Autovacuum does this continuously; failure to freeze forces an anti-wraparound shutdown. The visibility map tracks all-visible/all-frozen pages, enabling index-only scans and vacuum skipping.

**First-updater-wins.** Under REPEATABLE READ, a writer that finds a concurrent committed xmax on its target row aborts with a serialization failure; under READ COMMITTED it re-fetches the latest version (`EvalPlanQual` recheck).

## 2. InnoDB (MySQL): undo-log rollback segments + read views

**Version storage.** InnoDB updates in place in the clustered index and writes the pre-image to **undo logs** stored in **rollback segments**. Each record carries hidden columns:

- **DB_TRX_ID**: ID of the last transaction that modified the record.
- **DB_ROLL_PTR**: pointer to the undo log record for the prior version, forming a backward version chain reconstructed on demand.
- **DB_ROW_ID**: synthetic row id if no PK exists.

Undo records are classified as insert undo (purgeable immediately at commit) and update undo (needed for consistent reads; retained until no read view needs them, then removed by the **purge** threads — InnoDB's analogue of vacuum). Long-running transactions pin undo history (visible as a growing history list length).

**Read views.** A consistent read uses a **read view** containing: the low/high watermark trx IDs and the list of active transactions at view creation. A record version is visible if `DB_TRX_ID` is below the low watermark or committed before the view; otherwise InnoDB walks the roll-pointer chain applying undo records until it reconstructs a visible version. REPEATABLE READ (default) creates one read view at the first read; READ COMMITTED creates one per statement. Note InnoDB REPEATABLE READ is snapshot-based for plain reads but **locking reads** (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, DML) read the latest version with **next-key locks** (record + gap locks) to prevent phantoms — a hybrid of MVCC and 2PL rather than pure SI.

## 3. Oracle: consistent read via rollback/undo segments

Oracle pioneered this design: **statement-level read consistency** always, with optional transaction-level consistency (SERIALIZABLE, which is actually snapshot isolation). Mechanism:

- Every change records before-images in **undo segments** (automatic undo management; historically "rollback segments").
- Each data block's ITL (interested transaction list) entries reference transactions and undo; the system clock is the **SCN (System Change Number)**, a monotonically increasing logical commit timestamp.
- A query is assigned a snapshot SCN. If a block contains changes with SCN newer than the snapshot (or uncommitted changes), Oracle clones the block and applies undo records to roll it back — producing a **consistent read (CR) block** in the buffer cache, i.e., block-level version reconstruction rather than tuple chains.
- If required undo has been overwritten (bounded by `UNDO_RETENTION`), the query fails with **ORA-01555 "snapshot too old"** — the classic symptom of bounded version retention.
- Writers use row-level locks recorded in block ITLs; "readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers." SERIALIZABLE enforces first-committer-wins via ORA-08177 ("can't serialize access").

## 4. SSI: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (Cahill et al. 2008; Ports & Grittner 2012, PostgreSQL)

Plain snapshot isolation admits anomalies absent from serializability, notably **write skew** (two transactions read overlapping data and make disjoint writes that are jointly inconsistent) and the batch/read-only anomaly. Fekete et al. showed every SI anomaly's serialization graph contains a **dangerous structure**: two consecutive **rw-antidependency** edges (rw-conflicts, where T1 reads a version that T2 concurrently overwrites) `T1 →rw T2 →rw T3`, with T3 (the "pivot" chain's endpoint) committing first.

**SSI mechanism** (Cahill/Röhm/Fekete; productionized by Ports & Grittner in PostgreSQL 9.1):

- Run transactions under SI, additionally tracking rw-antidependencies using **SIREAD locks** — non-blocking predicate read markers (in PostgreSQL: tuple/page/relation granularity, promotable under memory pressure), retained *after* commit until concurrent transactions finish.
- Each transaction tracks inConflict/outConflict flags (PostgreSQL tracks the conflict edges). When a transaction would become the pivot of a dangerous structure (both an incoming and outgoing rw-antidependency with a committed endpoint), one transaction is aborted with a **serialization failure** (SQLSTATE 40001); apps must retry.
- This is conservative (false positives — some aborted schedules were actually serializable) but sound, and avoids the blocking of strict 2PL and the read validation cost of classical OCC. PostgreSQL adds a **safe snapshot** optimization: `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` waits for a snapshot guaranteed anomaly-free, then needs no SIREAD tracking.

## 5. Hekaton (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP): timestamp-ordered MVCC

Larson et al. (2011/2012): a fully in-memory, latch-free engine.

- Each row version carries a **begin timestamp** and **end timestamp** defining its validity interval `[begin, end)`. A version is visible to a transaction reading at logical time RT iff `begin ≤ RT < end`.
- Transactions get a **begin timestamp** (read time) from a monotonic global counter and, at commit, a **commit timestamp** that determines serialization order. While a writer is uncommitted, the begin/end field temporarily holds its transaction ID; readers resolve it against the transaction's state (**speculative reads/commit dependencies**: a reader may take a dependency on an uncommitted writer's outcome rather than block).
- Writes install new versions via compare-and-swap on latch-free Bw-tree/hash indexes; write-write conflicts abort the second writer (first-writer-wins, no lock waits).
- Serializability is achieved **optimistically**: at commit, under SERIALIZABLE the engine **validates** by re-checking read-set versions are still visible at the commit timestamp and re-executing scans to detect phantoms; REPEATABLE READ validates reads only; SNAPSHOT needs no validation.
- Garbage collection is cooperative and parallel: versions whose end timestamp precedes the oldest active transaction's read time are unreachable and reclaimed by worker threads and by threads that encounter garbage during scans.

---

# Logical Clocks

Physical clocks on distinct machines cannot be perfectly synchronized, so distributed systems order events using logical mechanisms grounded in causality.

## Happened-before relation (Lamport 1978)

Lamport's **happened-before** relation `→` is the smallest transitive relation such that: (a) if a and b are events in the same process and a precedes b, then a → b; (b) if a is the send of a message and b its receipt, a → b; (c) transitivity. Events with neither a → b nor b → a are **concurrent** (a ∥ b). This is the causal partial order all logical clocks approximate; a correct clock C must satisfy the **clock condition**: a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b).

## 1. Lamport clocks (scalar logical clocks)

Each process keeps an integer counter L:

- On each local event: `L := L + 1`.
- On send: increment, attach L to the message.
- On receive with timestamp Lm: `L := max(L, Lm) + 1`.

Guarantees the clock condition (a → b ⇒ L(a) < L(b)) but **not the converse**: L(a) < L(b) does not imply causality — concurrent events still get ordered timestamps, and you cannot detect concurrency. Breaking ties with process IDs yields a **total order** consistent with happened-before, used in Lamport's mutual exclusion algorithm and as the conceptual basis for timestamp ordering and state machine replication.

## 2. Vector clocks (Fidge/Mattern 1988) — Dynamo/Riak

Each of N processes keeps a vector V[1..N]:

- Local event at process i: `V[i] += 1`.
- Send: attach V; Receive: elementwise `V := max(V, Vm)`, then `V[i] += 1`.

Comparison: V(a) < V(b) iff V(a) ≤ V(b) componentwise and V(a) ≠ V(b). Vector clocks **characterize causality exactly**: `a → b ⇔ V(a) < V(b)`; incomparable vectors mean concurrent events. This strong property (Charron-Bost proved Θ(N) entries are necessary) costs O(N) metadata per event.

**Dynamo/Riak usage.** Amazon's Dynamo attaches a vector clock (per-object, indexed by coordinator node rather than client — technically a *version vector* variant) to each object version. On read, if versions are causally ordered, obsolete ones are discarded (**syntactic reconciliation**); if concurrent (vector-incomparable), all **siblings** are returned for **semantic reconciliation** by the application (e.g., shopping-cart merge). Dynamo truncates clocks beyond a size threshold (clock pruning), trading precision for bounded metadata. Riak followed the same model and later moved to **dotted version vectors** (Preguiça/Almeida et al.) to correctly track concurrent client writes through the same server and avoid false concurrency/sibling explosion.

## 3. Hybrid Logical Clocks (Kulkarni, Demirbas et al. 2014) — CockroachDB

HLC combines physical time's meaningfulness with logical causality. Each node keeps `(l, c)` where l tracks the maximum physical time seen (from local clock pt or received messages) and c is a logical counter for tie-breaking:

- Local/send event: `l' := max(l, pt)`; if `l' = l` then `c += 1` else `c := 0`.
- Receive (m carries l_m, c_m): `l' := max(l, l_m, pt)`; c set to max(+1) of whichever components equal l', else 0.

Properties: satisfies the clock condition (e → f ⇒ hlc(e) < hlc(f)); l stays within the clock-synchronization error ε of true physical time (`pt ≤ l ≤ pt + ε` under bounded skew); c is bounded; fits in 64 bits (physical bits + counter bits); monotonic even across NTP adjustments; **backward compatible with NTP timestamps** and never blocks waiting on clocks.

**CockroachDB usage.** HLC timestamps order MVCC versions and define transaction read/write timestamps. Causal dependencies propagated via messages are captured by HLC, so related transactions order correctly without synchronized clocks. CockroachDB enforces a **maximum clock offset** (default 500 ms): a read that encounters a value with timestamp in its **uncertainty interval** `(read_ts, read_ts + max_offset]` performs an **uncertainty restart** (possibly at a higher timestamp), ensuring single-key linearizability-like guarantees; CockroachDB provides serializable isolation overall but not strict external consistency across all transactions (no "stale read of causally-later write" only when causality flows through the system or clocks are within bounds).

## 4. TrueTime (Google Spanner) — a bounded-uncertainty physical clock

TrueTime is not a logical clock but a **bounded-uncertainty clock API**: `TT.now()` returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain absolute time; `TT.after(t)` / `TT.before(t)` are derived predicates. Implementation: per-datacenter time masters with **GPS receivers and atomic clocks**, cross-checked (Marzullo-style agreement rejecting liars); client daemons poll masters and grow uncertainty ε between polls based on worst-case local oscillator drift (~200 µs/s), yielding typical ε of ~1–7 ms.

**Commit wait.** Spanner achieves **external consistency** (strict serializability: if T1 commits in real time before T2 starts, T1's commit timestamp < T2's): the coordinator picks commit timestamp `s ≥ TT.now().latest`, then **waits until `TT.after(s)` is true** (i.e., s has definitely passed everywhere) before releasing locks and acknowledging. Thus timestamp order matches real-time order globally. Small ε makes commit wait cheap and often overlapped with Paxos replication latency.

TrueTime also enables **snapshot reads** at any timestamp t once replicas' safe time passes t, and lock-free consistent global reads — doing with real-time intervals what logical clocks do with causal metadata, at the cost of specialized hardware. HLC is frequently described as the commodity-hardware alternative: it provides causal consistency unconditionally and approximates TrueTime's ordering within the clock-offset bound, but cannot guarantee external consistency between causally unrelated transactions without waiting.

## Comparison summary

| Mechanism | Ordering guarantee | Detects concurrency? | Metadata | Hardware needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lamport clock | a→b ⇒ L(a)<L(b) (one-way) | No | O(1) scalar | None |
| Vector clock | a→b ⇔ V(a)<V(b) (exact) | Yes | O(N) | None |
| HLC | Clock condition + physical closeness within ε | No (scalar-like) | 64 bits | NTP-class sync |
| TrueTime | Real-time intervals ⇒ external consistency via commit wait | N/A (real time) | Interval | GPS + atomic clocks |

response.content:
# Findings: LSM Trees and B+Tree Maintenance

## (3) Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees

### Core architecture: memtable + SSTables + WAL

- **Memtable**: an in-memory, mutable, sorted structure (typically a skip list, as in RocksDB's default `SkipListRep`, or a red-black tree) that absorbs all writes. Writes are first appended to a **write-ahead log (WAL)** for durability, then inserted into the memtable — making every write a sequential-I/O operation, the central LSM advantage.
- **Flush**: when the memtable reaches a size threshold (e.g., RocksDB `write_buffer_size`), it is marked **immutable** and flushed to disk as an **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** — an immutable file of key-ordered key-value pairs with a block index, per-block checksums, and typically a per-file Bloom filter. RocksDB can hold multiple immutable memtables (`max_write_buffer_number`) to decouple foreground writes from flush I/O.
- **Deletes** are logical: a **tombstone** record is written and physically purged only when compaction reaches the bottommost level containing the key (Cassandra additionally gates purge on `gc_grace_seconds` to avoid resurrecting data via anti-entropy repair).
- **Reads** must merge across components: memtable(s) → L0 SSTables (which may have overlapping key ranges) → deeper levels, newest-to-oldest, returning the first match. Range scans use a **merging iterator** (k-way merge over heap of per-component iterators).

### Compaction strategies

**Leveled compaction (LCS; RocksDB's default, modeled on LevelDB):**
- Levels L1…Ln each hold a run of **non-overlapping SSTables**, with each level ~10× (configurable `max_bytes_for_level_multiplier`) larger than the previous. L0 is special: files there are whole flushed memtables and may overlap.
- When level Li exceeds its target size, a victim SSTable is merged with the **overlapping SSTables in Li+1**, rewriting them. Because each level is a single sorted run, a point read touches at most one SSTable per level (plus all of L0).
- Properties: low **read amplification** (≈ one file per level) and low **space amplification** (~10% overhead at steady state, since ~90% of data sits in the bottom level and stale versions are bounded), but high **write amplification** — each key is rewritten once per level, so WA ≈ fanout × number of levels (commonly 10–30×).

**Size-tiered compaction (STCS; Cassandra's classic default, also RocksDB "universal" compaction):**
- SSTables are grouped into **tiers** of similar size; when `min_threshold` (default 4) similarly sized SSTables accumulate, they are merged into one larger SSTable in the next tier.
- Properties: low **write amplification** (each key rewritten ~once per tier, O(log N) total), but higher **read amplification** (multiple overlapping runs per tier must be checked) and poor **space amplification** — transiently up to 2× during a major compaction (need space for inputs + output), and stale versions of a key can persist across many tiers. Suits write-heavy, scan-light workloads.
- Cassandra alternatives: **LCS** (read-heavy), **TWCS (Time-Window Compaction Strategy)** for time-series data (buckets SSTables by time window so whole-SSTable expiry via TTL avoids compaction entirely), and the newer **UCS (Unified Compaction Strategy)** which parameterizes the tiered↔leveled continuum via a scaling factor (per Dayan & Idreos's *Dostoevsky*/lazy-leveling analysis).

### Bloom filters

- Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** over its keys (RocksDB: per-block or full-file filter via `BloomFilterPolicy`, typically ~10 bits/key → ~1% false-positive rate). A point lookup probes the filter before touching the file's index/data blocks, eliminating almost all I/O for keys absent from that SSTable — this is what makes STCS's and L0's many overlapping runs tolerable for point reads.
- Limitations: no help for **range queries** (RocksDB addresses this with **prefix Bloom filters**; SuRF-style succinct range filters are a research alternative) and false positives still cost I/O. RocksDB also supports **ribbon filters** as a space-efficient replacement.
- Complementary structures: **fence pointers** (per-block sparse index / partitioned index) bound within-file search to one block.

### The RUM tradeoff: write / read / space amplification

- **Write amplification (WA)**: total bytes written to storage ÷ bytes of user data. Leveled ≫ tiered. Matters for SSD endurance and write bandwidth.
- **Read amplification (RA)**: storage accesses (or sorted runs consulted) per query. Tiered ≫ leveled; Bloom filters mitigate point-read RA but not range RA.
- **Space amplification (SA)**: physical ÷ logical size. Tiered ≫ leveled (stale versions across runs; 2× transient during merge).
- You can optimize at most two; this is formalized in the **RUM conjecture** (Athanassoulis et al.) and tuned continuously by **Monkey/Dostoevsky** (Dayan & Idreos): allocate Bloom-filter bits non-uniformly across levels and mix tiering (upper levels) with leveling (bottom level, "lazy leveling") to Pareto-improve the tradeoff.

### WiscKey: key-value separation

- **WiscKey** (Lu et al., FAST '16) stores values in a separate append-only **value log (vLog)**; the LSM tree holds only keys plus `<vLog offset, size>` pointers. Since compaction then rewrites only small key-pointer entries, write amplification drops dramatically for large values (e.g., ~10× reduction at 1 KB values), and the LSM stays small enough to cache, improving point reads.
- Costs: **range scans** lose locality (values are scattered in the vLog) — WiscKey compensates with **parallel prefetching** exploiting SSD internal parallelism; and the vLog requires its own **garbage collection** (walk the log, re-query the LSM for liveness, relocate live values to the head, punch-hole/truncate the tail), which adds back some write cost and complexity around crash consistency.
- Production descendants: **RocksDB BlobDB** (integrated blob files), **Titan** (TiKV), **Badger** (Dgraph). A common refinement is a size threshold (`min_blob_size`): small values stay inline in the LSM, large ones go to the blob/value log.

---

## (4) B+Tree Maintenance

### Structure recap

All records live in **leaf nodes**, chained in a doubly (or singly) linked **leaf sibling list** for range scans; internal nodes hold only **separator keys** and child pointers. Order/fanout d; invariant: every node except the root stays between 50% (⌈d/2⌉) and 100% full.

### Node splits, merges, and rebalancing

- **Split (insert overflow)**: inserting into a full leaf splits it into two half-full nodes; a copy of the split key (**separator**) is **pushed up** into the parent. If the parent overflows, the split **propagates**; a root split adds a level — B+trees grow at the root, keeping all leaves at equal depth (perfectly height-balanced). Note the leaf/internal asymmetry: leaf splits **copy up** the separator; internal splits **push up** (the middle key moves, it isn't duplicated).
- **Merge/coalesce (delete underflow)**: when a deletion drops a node below minimum occupancy, it is merged with a sibling if their combined entries fit in one node; the separator in the parent is removed (and for internal merges, **pulled down** into the merged node). Underflow can propagate upward; collapsing the root's last child shrinks tree height.
- **Sibling redistribution (borrowing/rotation)**: the cheaper alternative to merging — if an adjacent sibling has spare entries (> minimum), move one or more entries across and **update the separator key in the parent** instead of restructuring. Preferred because it touches only three nodes with no structural modification. Many production engines (e.g., classic System R–descended designs, and effectively PostgreSQL) skip eager merging entirely: underfull pages are tolerated and only fully empty pages are deleted/reclaimed (**lazy deletion / free-at-empty**), justified empirically because workloads rarely shrink monotonically.

### Blink-trees (Lehman–Yao)

- Each node carries a **right-link (right-sibling pointer)** and a **high key** (upper bound on keys in the node). A split is decomposed into two atomic half-steps: (1) create the right sibling and set the left node's right-link and high key; (2) later insert the new separator into the parent.
- Between the half-steps the tree is temporarily "inconsistent," but any concurrent reader that descends into the old node and finds its search key > high key simply **follows the right-link** ("move right") to recover — so readers need **no lock coupling at all** in the original Lehman–Yao design, and writers lock at most a constant number of nodes. This eliminates the need to hold ancestor latches during splits.
- Used in **PostgreSQL's nbtree** (with additions: left-links for backward scans, and page-deletion protocol by Lanin–Shasha-style techniques).

### Latch coupling / crabbing

- **Latch coupling (hand-over-hand / crabbing)**: during descent, acquire the child's latch before releasing the parent's. Readers take shared latches; writers take exclusive latches.
- **Pessimistic protocol**: a writer holds exclusive latches on all ancestors that might be modified, releasing an ancestor only when the current node is **"safe"** (not full for inserts; above minimum for deletes), since a safe node absorbs any propagation.
- **Optimistic protocol (optimistic lock coupling / OLC in modern terms)**: descend with shared latches (or latch-free version validation via per-node version counters, as in HyPer/LeanStore's OLC) assuming the leaf is safe; take exclusive only at the leaf; **restart with the pessimistic protocol** if a split/merge is actually needed. Blink-trees go further and avoid held-across-split latches entirely via right-links.

### Prefix compression and fill factor

- **Prefix compression (prefix truncation)**: within a page, store the **common key prefix once** and only suffixes per slot (e.g., InnoDB page-level prefix compression, PostgreSQL deduplication-adjacent techniques). Related: **suffix truncation** (Bayer–Unterauer "prefix B-trees") — a separator posted to the parent needs only the **shortest key that distinguishes** the two children, not a full key; both techniques raise effective fanout and reduce height.
- **Fill factor**: target page occupancy at load/split time. Random-insert B+trees converge to ~69% (ln 2) average occupancy via 50/50 splits. For **monotonically increasing keys** (sequence IDs, timestamps), engines use a **rightmost-leaf split heuristic** (split 90/10 or simply start a fresh page — PostgreSQL default `fillfactor=90` for the rightmost split; InnoDB's sequential-insert optimization) to achieve near-100% packing instead of 50% waste. Lower fill factor deliberately leaves slack to absorb future random inserts/HOT updates and defer splits.

### Bulk loading

- Rather than N individual inserts (O(N log N) with random I/O and split churn), **bulk loading** sorts all keys externally, writes **packed leaf pages left-to-right at the chosen fill factor**, then builds internal levels bottom-up from the leaves' separator keys. One sequential pass, no splits, perfect page utilization, and clustered leaves. This is how `CREATE INDEX` works in PostgreSQL (external sort via tuplesort, then bottom-up build) and most engines; deferred/merged index builds in LSM-backed engines are the analogous idea.

### Write-optimized B+tree variants

- **Fractal trees / Bε-trees** (TokuDB/TokuMX, PerconaFT): every internal node has a **message buffer**; inserts/deletes/updates are encoded as messages deposited at the root and **flushed down lazily in batches** when a buffer fills. This amortizes one I/O over many operations, giving asymptotically better insert cost — O(logB N / εB^(1−ε)) amortized vs. O(logB N) for a B-tree — while keeping B-tree-like point-query cost. Queries must apply pending messages on the root-to-leaf path.
- **Bw-tree** (Microsoft Hekaton/SQL Server, Levandoski et al.): a **latch-free** B+tree for multicore/SSD. Nodes are logical page IDs resolved through a **mapping table**; updates **prepend delta records** (insert/delete/split deltas) to a node's delta chain via a single **CAS** on the mapping-table entry — no in-place writes, no latches. Chains are periodically **consolidated** into a fresh base page. Structure modifications (splits) follow a Blink-style two-phase protocol with split deltas and parent-index-term deltas; pairs naturally with log-structured storage (LLAMA).
- Honorable mention: **Masstree** (trie of B+trees for long keys) and **ART-hybrid** designs occupy adjacent points but are not strictly B+tree variants.

### Summary contrast with LSM

B+trees update in place with O(log_B N) read and write I/O and no background compaction, giving predictable reads and good range-scan locality; LSM trees convert random writes to sequential ones at the cost of compaction-driven write amplification and multi-run read amplification mitigated by Bloom filters. Bε-trees/Bw-trees sit between the two on the read/write-optimization spectrum.
